summary: Specifies DNS64, which creates AAAA records from A records so IPv6-only clients can reach IPv4-only servers through a translator. It also gives deployment suggestions. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If a name only has an old-style address, this makes up a new-style one that leads to a translator, so the new-style device can still visit.

questions: synthesize aaaa records from a records
how does dns64 synthesize aaaa records
subtitle: How a DNS server invents IPv6 addresses for IPv4-only servers so IPv6-only clients can still reach them by name.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only client asks the DNS for the IPv6 address (a AAAA record) of a server that only has an IPv4 address (an A record), and gets nothing useful back.
tldr.mechanism: DNS64 looks up the A record when no AAAA record exists and builds a synthetic AAAA record from it, embedding the IPv4 address in an IPv6 prefix that an IPv6/IPv4 translator is configured to handle.
tldr.outcome: Together with a translator such as stateful NAT64, an IPv6-only client can start communication by name with an IPv4-only server without any change to either node. The catch is that it interacts badly with DNSSEC validation and with hosts that have several networks.

facts.label: Fallback TTL
facts.value: A record TTL or 600 seconds, whichever is shorter

today: RFC 6147 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the specification of DNS64. It is meant to be used with a translator such as stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146).

sections.title: The Problem DNS64 Solves
sections.content:
RFC 6147 specifies DNS64, a mechanism that is part of the toolbox for IPv4-IPv6 transition and coexistence. Used together with an IPv6/IPv4 translator such as stateful NAT64 (RFC 6146), it lets an IPv6-only client start communication by name with an IPv4-only server.

The mechanism works by synthesizing AAAA resource records from A records. A synthetic AAAA record keeps the owner name of the original A record, but holds an IPv6 address instead of an IPv4 address. That IPv6 address is generated by an algorithm from the IPv4 address and a few configured parameters, typically an IPv6 prefix.

The RFC expects this to matter because of IPv4 address depletion: many IPv6-only clients will want to reach IPv4-only servers. In the typical case only the translators and one or more DNS64-enabled name servers have to be deployed. Some features need the DNS64 function inside the end hosts themselves.
sections.eli5: Some computers only understand the new kind of address, but some websites only have the old kind. DNS64 makes up a new-style address that leads to a translator, so the two can still talk.

sections.title: How DNS64 and the Translator Fit Together
sections.content:
The translator sits between an IPv6 network and an IPv4 network. DNS64 appears to the IPv6 client as an ordinary DNS server or resolver. When it receives a AAAA query it first tries to resolve the real AAAA records. If there are none, which is the normal case for an IPv4-only target, it queries for A records and creates one synthetic AAAA record for each A record it finds.

The synthetic address contains a prefix called Pref64::/n and also embeds the original IPv4 address. The same algorithm and the same prefix must be configured in both the DNS64 and the translator, so each can generate the same IPv6 representation of a given IPv4 address. IPv6 packets addressed to that prefix must also be delivered to a translator that has the prefix configured. There is no communication between the DNS64 and the translator: the shared state is just the prefix and an optional set of static parameters.

Two kinds of prefix can be used. The Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 is reserved by RFC 6052 for representing IPv4 addresses in IPv6. A Network-Specific Prefix (NSP) is a prefix that an organization assigns for the purpose and controls locally.

The DNS64 function can live in three places:

  • In authoritative servers for a zone, which then provide synthetic records for IPv4-only hosts in that zone.
  • In recursive name servers that serve end hosts ("recursive-resolver mode"). Current IPv6 nodes can use this without modification.
  • In the end host, coupled to its stub resolver ("stub-resolver mode"). It works with DNSSEC validation in the host, but needs changes to end hosts.
sections.eli5: The helper and the translator agree on a secret pattern ahead of time. The helper writes addresses in that pattern, and the translator knows how to read them back. They never have to talk to each other.

sections.title: Answering a AAAA Query
sections.content:
DNS64 first tries to get real AAAA records for the class IN query, possibly from a local cache. If real data exists, it is returned as usual, and by default DNS64 implementations MUST NOT synthesize records when real AAAA records exist. An exclusion set lets an operator mark prefixes as unusable. Addresses in ::ffff:0:0/96 are one example, and an implementation SHOULD include that range by default. A AAAA answer containing only excluded addresses is treated as empty, and excluded records MUST NOT be returned.

Errors are handled this way: RCODE 3 (Name Error) is passed on as normal DNS behavior, any other non-zero RCODE is treated as an empty answer, and a timeout is treated as RCODE 2 (Server failure). CNAME and DNAME chains are followed to the first A or AAAA record and are included in the final answer.

If the answer is empty, DNS64 asks for A records and, if it gets some, builds the synthetic records and returns them in the answer section in place of the A records. It MAY send the AAAA and A queries in parallel to save time, at the cost of unneeded A queries when no synthesis is needed. Each synthetic record is built like this:

  • NAME is copied from the A record, TYPE is 28 (AAAA), CLASS is 1 and RDLENGTH is 16.
  • TTL is the minimum of the A record's TTL and the SOA record's TTL for the queried domain. If no SOA record came with the negative answer, DNS64 SHOULD use the A record's TTL or 600 seconds, whichever is shorter.
  • RDATA is the IPv6 representation of the IPv4 address.

Other records are handled as follows. A DNS64 server answers PTR queries for addresses in the prefixes it uses, either by answering authoritatively itself or by synthesizing a CNAME that points into the IPv4 reverse tree; it must provide one of the two. DNS64 MUST NOT synthesize records in the additional section, and all other records are returned unchanged.
sections.eli5: The helper first checks whether the website has a new-style address. Only if it does not, the helper looks up the old-style one and rewrites it in the new style.

sections.title: Building the IPv6 Address
sections.content:
DNS64 can support several algorithms for turning an IPv4 address into an IPv6 one, but they must obey three constraints. The same algorithm MUST be used by the DNS64 and by the translator. The algorithm MUST be reversible, so the original IPv4 address can be recovered from the IPv6 form. And its input MUST be limited to the IPv4 address, the prefix, and optionally a set of stable parameters configured in both places, such as a fixed suffix.

Each prefix Pref64::/n MUST have n less than or equal to 96. If any prefixes are configured, the default algorithm MUST use them and not the Well-Known Prefix. If none is available it MUST use 64:ff9b::/96. A DNS64 MUST support the algorithm in Section 2 of RFC 6052, and that algorithm MUST be the default. The implementation SHOULD also support mapping separate IPv4 address ranges to separate IPv6 prefixes, which allows handling of special-use IPv4 addresses.
sections.eli5: The address rewrite follows a recipe that can be run backwards. Both the helper and the translator use the same recipe, so the translator can always figure out the original address.

sections.title: Deployment Pitfalls
sections.content:
The RFC warns that DNS64 is incompatible with some things deployed in IPv4-only or dual-stack settings. A full-service resolver that is unaware of DNS64 and is configured as a mixed-mode iterative and forwarding resolver cannot be made to work properly, because it will likely get IPv4-only glue records and then be unable to answer the needed AAAA queries. An existing DNSSEC validator that does not know about DNS64 may reject all the data as tampered with, so validation behind a DNS64 needs a validator that performs the DNS64 function itself, or a trusted connection to a validating DNS64 resolver.

Hosts with more than one network cause trouble because a synthetic address only works through the network where it was made. If one interface reaches the IPv4 Internet through a NAT64 and another has native IPv6 only, an answer received on the first interface will not connect on the second. The RFC says it is generally preferable for hosts to treat DNS answers from one interface as local to that interface.

If a dual-stack host has native IPv4 on another interface, it may prefer IPv6 by default and send traffic through the NAT64 when native IPv4 would be better. Hosts with IPv4 connectivity to the Internet should avoid using DNS64, and operators of a NAT64 should expect traffic to pass through it even when it is not necessary. If the other interface only reaches a local LAN, DNS64 must not synthesize records for hosts in that LAN, or else must give context-sensitive ("split view") answers.
sections.eli5: The made-up address only works on the road where it was made. A computer that has two roads can end up picking the wrong one and getting stuck.

sections.title: Worked Deployment Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through three scenarios. In the first, an IPv6 host H1 in an IPv6-only site contacts an IPv4 host H2 (h2.example.com, address 192.0.2.1) on the IPv4 Internet. The recursive name server does the DNS64 work and finds no AAAA records. It then gets the A record and returns 64:ff9b::192.0.2.1, built from the Well-Known Prefix in the upper 96 bits and the IPv4 address in the lower 32 bits. H1 sends its packet to that address and it is routed to the translator.

In the second, the DNS64 function runs inside H1's stub resolver while the recursive server does no DNS64. The recursive server returns an empty answer to the AAAA query, H1 then asks for the A record, and its own DNS64 function builds the same 64:ff9b::192.0.2.1.

In the third, an IPv6 host on the IPv6 Internet contacts an IPv4 site that uses the Network-Specific Prefix 2001:db8::/96. The RFC's recommended approach here is to assign fixed IPv6 addresses to the IPv4 nodes and publish real AAAA records, with no synthesis at query time. For dynamic setups where DNS Update changes the A records, synthesizing when the update arrives is preferred over synthesizing when a query arrives. Query-time synthesis, which gives 2001:db8::192.0.2.1, is described for cases where the primary server cannot be upgraded but a secondary can.
sections.eli5: In each story, the helper turns an old-style address into a new-style one that starts with an agreed pattern, and the packet then goes to the translator.

sections.title: DNSSEC and Prefix Security
sections.content:
DNS64 changes DNS answers, and DNSSEC exists to detect changed answers, so the two can collide. What happens depends on two bits in the query. The DO bit says the client understands DNSSEC data, and the CD bit says it wants all the data so it can check for itself.

A validating resolver that also does DNS64 (the RFC calls it vDNS64) behaves as follows. It MUST validate the negative AAAA answer before asking for A records. Skipping this would let an attacker use DNS64 to get around DNSSEC. If the data does not validate, it MUST respond with RCODE 2. When CD is set and DO is set, vDNS64 MUST NOT perform synthesis and must return the data so the client can do the validation and the synthesis itself. Any endpoint that wants to validate in a NAT64 context must therefore be translation-aware.

There is a second risk. The DNS64 and the NAT64 must use the same Pref64. If an attacker changes the prefix used by the DNS64, the host's traffic goes to the altered prefix. That can cause a denial-of-service attack, a flooding attack against devices that do not want the traffic, or eavesdropping if the prefix is routed through the attacker.
sections.eli5: Security checks look for any answer that was changed on the way. The helper changes answers on purpose, so it has to be careful not to confuse those checks. Also, if a bad person changes the secret pattern, the packets go to the wrong place.
